title: The monk Dharmakara
hook: a monk in the distant past makes his vows to create a land where all can awaken (Larger Sukhavati-vyuha)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sukhavati: the land of bliss, far to the west, where nobody turns back from the path. Your line was the land of bliss. What place did you notice that makes kindness easier? Day one thousand two hundred fifty-six.

A king is sitting in a crowd, listening to a Buddha teach. This is a story the Buddha tells his attendant Ananda in the longer sutra on the land of bliss, and it happens in ages so far back the sutra has to stack one past age on another to reach it. The Buddha teaching is named Lokeshvararaja. The king hears him, and something lands so deep that he gives up his throne, takes the robe, and becomes a monk. His new name is Dharmakara. And this monk is about to ask his teacher for something enormous.
screen: `A KING IN THE CROWD.` → `HE GIVES UP THE THRONE.` → `THE MONK DHARMAKARA.`

segments.voice: First, the change. The story begins with a king becoming a monk, and that's the whole pattern in miniature: giving up one kind of power to take on another kind of work. Second, the request. Dharmakara asks his teacher to show him the lands of the Buddhas, the fine ones and the poor ones, so that he can make a land of his own that gathers up what is best. His teacher shows him. Then the monk goes quiet. In the sutra he spends an immense stretch of time just thinking it through, before he says a word. Third, the vows. He comes back to his teacher and speaks them aloud, one by one, and they share one shape. When I become a Buddha, if my land still holds realms of suffering, may I not attain perfect awakening. When I become a Buddha, if the beings born there do not reach awakening, may I not attain it either. Each vow ends the same way. If not, not me. In the version of the sutra read in China and Japan, there are forty-eight of them. Fourth, why the shape matters. A usual bargain says: first I'll get mine, then I'll help. Dharmakara's vows run the other way. He ties his own awakening to everyone else's. He refuses to count himself finished while the land he promised isn't real. The sutra says the vows were fulfilled: Dharmakara became a Buddha, and his land is the land of bliss. Who he became gets a day of its own.
screen: `A KING BECOMES A MONK.` · `SHOW ME THE LANDS.` · `IF NOT, MAY I NOT AWAKEN.` · `HIS AWAKENING TIED TO EVERYONE'S.` · then, large: `FORTY-EIGHT VOWS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Choose one small, concrete thing you'll do for someone else this week: a call, a ride, a meal, an hour of listening. Give it Dharmakara's shape, in your own words: I won't call this week finished until it's done. Say it once, silently. Then sit with it, breathing, and let the vow settle in your body, not as pressure but as a promise you've decided to keep. The bell holds the time.
The monk Dharmakara: a king who became a monk, studied the lands of the Buddhas, and vowed not to accept awakening unless his land would carry others to it. Today's word.
Your line: forty-eight vows. Today, keep the one vow you made for someone else, and notice how it shapes the rest of your day. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Pure Land Buddhists chant and study the longer sutra on the land of bliss, in which the monk Dharmakara makes his vows; in East Asia the vows are counted as forty-eight, and temples and teachers return to them often.

original.note: Sanskrit: Dharmakara, rendered 'treasury of the dharma'. in Japanese he is Hozo (法蔵).

trapdoor: what you thought: a holy man in an old legend.
what it means: a king turned monk whose vows built a land where all can awaken.
what a scholar hears: vows that all share one shape: if this is not so, may I not attain perfect awakening.

sources.ref: Larger Sukhavati-vyuha (Sutra of Immeasurable Life): Dharmakara's story and vows

notes: The carry 'forty-eight vows' follows the Chinese version (Sutra of Immeasurable Life). Sanskrit and Tibetan versions number the vows differently; the script says so. Confirm phrasing.
Vow wording is paraphrased; the two examples loosely follow the first vow (no evil realms) and the eleventh (beings there reach awakening). Confirm.
Dharmakara's teacher named as Lokeshvararaja (Sejizaio); the king's renunciation and the long period of reflection follow the sutra; specific numbers of lands and ages are deliberately omitted.
Gloss 'treasury of the dharma' for Dharmakara and Japanese Hozo (法蔵): confirm.
Practice asks for a personal commitment in the listener's own words, not a liturgical vow.

Editor: first vow paraphrase corrected (the vow is that the land have no realms of suffering, not that beings there fall into them). Cut the manuscript claim that other versions number the vows differently from the myth reveal and trapdoor (the cited text does not say it); 'often rendered' trimmed.
